block_text: Céline's song is called On ne change pas – "we don't change." I think that's both fortunately, and unfortunately, true for most of us. Fortunately in the sense that the sweet, innocent, curious, vivacious little one is still inside us, even if hiding. Unfortunate in the sense that we often don't truly develop the adult qualities that we might pretend to have, so we continue burdening that little one inside us with troubles they aren't made for handling. This shows up in how we may feel abandoned, helpless, impulsive, frightened, or desperate to be chosen.

block_text: Those ghosts knew my weakness: dares. So they would dare me to jump out the window. I wasn't suicidal, but I hated to seem like a "wussy." Luckily, I trusted my parents with this information, and instead of taking me to a psychiatrist and pumping me full of anti-psychotic drugs, they put bars on the windows. Many kids are not so lucky in modern societies. They may get pumped full of anti-psychotic drugs for the rest of their life once diagnosed. That said, it'd make sense to get a professional to weigh in for some situations. I still played around with half-hanging out the windows, but I wasn't quite dumb enough to jump out, and I really appreciate that my parents took it seriously without catastrophizing.

section: Using spiritual attack for spiritual gain
block_text: Borrowing support like that is basically borrowed adulthood. At first you may need to feel protected or loved by something bigger than you, before that love starts to feel like yours, and then bit by bit it starts to become your own. Send some of it down to your frightened little one, and when that's possible, toward whatever you're afraid of. Continuing to relate to benevolent spiritual powers/beings is still perfectly fine, but they would surely be happy if they rubbed off on you! If you're Christian, remember that in John 14:12, Jesus told his disciples whoever believed in him would do greater works than he did.

section: How This Relates to Similar Therapies
block_text: My reparenting guide is part of the larger reparenting and inner child therapy category. As far as I can tell, it was first developed in 1976 by Dr. Lucia Capacchione. Although Lucia is no longer with us, her institute still trains therapists in her methods (including art therapy and other things). I greatly respect and appreciate what Lucia has given us to work with. While there are many inner child therapy offshoots (often less codified than Lucia's book, Recovery of Your Inner Child), it would be impossible for me to compare my guide to each individual therapist's approach. block_text: You can see both sides of this see-saw in the guru types who supposedly embody their Higher Self. Anthony de Mello) is an excellent example. He was a Jesuit priest who mixed stories from all kinds of traditions into his teaching on seeing through the ego's traps and coming back to the Perfect Present. He also had a background as a psychotherapist who understood trauma-informed healing methods. He seemed to drift between the two opposite paradigms in a way that contradicted itself. And that bizarre contradiction is itself cited as "crazy wisdom" by apologists.
